summary: Describes how the restrictions on the IPv6 flow label apply when it is used for load balancing by equal cost multipath routing and link aggregation. It focuses on IP-in-IPv6 tunnels, where the outer header can carry a label for spreading traffic across paths.

plainLanguage.summary: When many roads lead to the same place, cars can be spread out. The flow label helps keep one trip on one road. This explains using it for tunneled traffic.

subtitle: How tunnel endpoints can set the IPv6 flow label so routers spread tunneled traffic evenly across equal cost paths.

tldr.problem: Traffic inside an IP-in-IPv6 tunnel all shares the same outer addresses, so routers hashing on them send everything down one path.
tldr.mechanism: The sending tunnel endpoint sets the outer IPv6 flow label to a value derived per user flow, and routers include the flow label in their ECMP or LAG hash.
tldr.outcome: Tunneled traffic can be shared across equal cost paths without routers having to look inside the tunnel, and without breaking the flow label rules.

facts.label: Minimum router hash input
facts.value: Dest addr, source addr, flow label

today: RFC 6438 is a Proposed Standard, published November 2011, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It applies together with the revised flow label specification in RFC 6437.

sections.title: Sharing Traffic Over Equal Paths
sections.content:
When the routing system knows several paths between two nodes are equally good, it can share traffic among them. Two techniques are equal cost multipath (ECMP) routing and link aggregation (LAG). The goals are a roughly equal share on each path, avoiding out-of-order delivery within a flow, and minimizing idle time on a path whose queue is non-empty.

A lightweight approach forms a modulo(N) hash from header fields that stay the same for the whole flow, and uses the result to pick one of N paths. A uniform hash shares traffic roughly equally, and because all packets of a flow hash to the same value, they do not arrive out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have several equal roads, you can pick a road for each trip using a code made from the trip's details. The same trip always gets the same road, so its cars stay in order.

sections.title: Choosing Hash Input Fields
sections.content:
The RFC uses flow to mean packets identified either by source and destination address alone (the 2-tuple) or by those plus protocol, source port and destination port (the 5-tuple). The 2-tuple is enough to avoid reordering, but many implementations use the 5-tuple to spread load better. The protocol and port numbers total 40 bits, and ephemeral ports typically contribute 16 variable bits.

For IPv6 the 5-tuple is awkward to extract because of the variable placement and length of next-headers. Hardware might therefore cut the length of the fields it extracts. A GRE header, possibly with a key, creates a similar difficulty.
sections.plainLanguage: The code for picking a road can use just the sender and receiver, or also the exact doors used. More details spread things better, but they are harder to read off the envelope.

sections.title: The Tunnel Polarization Problem
sections.content:
In an IP-in-IP tunnel, nearly all hardware can only look at the outermost IP header. Traffic from many sources to many destinations is packed into one tunnel from tunnel endpoint (TEP) A to TEP B, so every packet has outer source A and outer destination B, and probably the same port and protocol numbers. The hash is then constant and no load sharing happens. The RFC calls this polarization. A high share of traffic from a few tunnels means partial polarization.

The 20-bit IPv6 flow label could replace the port and protocol numbers in the 5-tuple, which would simplify implementations, especially when the inner header is not reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: If every car in a convoy wears the same sticker, the signs cannot tell them apart and send all of them down one road.

sections.title: The Flow Label Rules
sections.content:
The flow label was left Experimental by RFC 2460 and better defined by RFC 3697. Three rules from RFC 3697 caused hesitation: the label set by the source MUST be delivered unchanged; nodes MUST NOT assume mathematical or other properties of the values; and router performance SHOULD NOT depend on the distribution of the values, since the bits alone make poor hash material.

Most nodes set the flow label to zero, which adds nothing to a hash but does no harm. In a tunnel, however, the TEP is itself the source of the outer packets, so it may freely set the outer flow label. Rules 2 and 3 assume routers need flow state set up, but routers R1 and R2 can rely on the labels being assigned by a known method. RFC 6437 revised RFC 3697 and obviates these concerns, and this document applies to both.
sections.plainLanguage: There were rules saying nobody on the way may change the sticker, and nobody may assume things about it. But the person who starts the convoy is the sender of the whole convoy, so that person can choose the sticker.

sections.title: Guidelines for the Sending Tunnel Endpoint
sections.content:
Inner packets MUST be encapsulated in an outer IPv6 packet whose addresses are those of the TEPs. The outer flow label SHOULD be a 20-bit value set in accordance with RFC 6437, and the same value MUST be used for all packets of one user flow. So the sending TEP MUST classify packets into flows and write the label into the outer header. It can identify a flow by the 2-tuple or the 5-tuple; the choice is an implementation matter.

The values should come from a uniform distribution, which suits a hash function and is hard for a third party to predict. The TEP MAY assign labels statelessly using a 20-bit hash of the inner header tuple, and may include the inner flow label if the inner packet is IPv6. Rarely, two user flows may share a label, which is acceptable because RFC 6437 lets a source define any set of packets as one flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender of the convoy gives each trip its own sticker, always the same one for the same trip, and picks sticker colors at random so they spread out.

sections.title: What Routers Do
sections.content:
The routers doing load distribution are assumed not to know they are handling tunneled traffic. Their hash MUST at minimum include the 3-tuple of destination address, source address and flow label, and MAY also include the rest of the 5-tuple. Because they see a mix of tunneled and normal traffic, the design should also include protocol and ports to add entropy for flows whose flow label is zero.

Individual nodes are free to use different algorithms that conform to this specification without harming interoperability. OAM techniques will need to be adapted to manage flow-label-based ECMP and LAG, with issues similar to those for MPLS (RFC 4379) and pseudowires (RFC 6391).
sections.plainLanguage: The road-sign robots just need to read the sender, the receiver and the sticker. If the sticker is blank, they also look at the other details.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The flow label is not protected and can be forged by an on-path attacker. The RFC expects tunnel endpoints and the ECMP or LAG paths to be part of a managed infrastructure well protected against such attacks, for example by using IPsec between the two tunnel endpoints. Off-path attackers are unlikely to guess a valid label if an apparently pseudo-random value is used. The worst an attacker could do is try to selectively overload one path. See RFC 6437 for more.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the road could swap stickers, but the worst they can do is crowd one road.
